After dinner the whole gang went out to look for turtle eggs on the sandbar. They prodded the sand with sticks, and whenever they found a soft patch, they knelt and dug with their hands. A single hole sometimes yielded fifty or sixty eggs. These were round and white, a little smaller than an English walnut. That evening they enjoyed a magnificent feast of fried eggs, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast they raced whooping and skipping onto the sandbar, chasing one another in circles and flinging off their clothes until they were naked. Then they carried their play far up the bar through the shallow water, pushing against a strong current that occasionally swept their legs from under them and made the fun even better. Now and again they crouched together and slapped water into one another’s faces with their palms. They edged closer, turning their faces away from the choking spray, until they caught hold of one another and wrestled. At last the strongest would force his neighbour underwater, and all three went down in a knot of pale arms and legs, emerging with a simultaneous burst of blowing, spluttering, laughter, and gasps for air.

When they were thoroughly exhausted, they ran out and stretched themselves on the hot, dry sand, lying there and burying themselves in it. Before long they dashed back into the water to repeat the whole performance. Finally they realized that their bare skin made quite a good substitute for flesh-coloured tights. They drew a circle in the sand and put on a circus with three clowns, since none of them would surrender that most distinguished role to anyone else.

Next they fetched their marbles and played knucks, ringtaw, and keeps until they tired of those games. Joe and Huck then went swimming again, but Tom refused to risk it. He had discovered that while kicking off his trousers, he had also kicked the string of rattlesnake rattles off his ankle. He wondered how he had escaped cramp for so long without that mysterious charm to protect him. He would not go back in until he found it, and by then the others were tired and wanted a rest. Gradually they drifted apart, grew gloomy, and stared longingly across the broad river toward the village dozing in the sunshine. Tom caught himself tracing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe. He rubbed it out, angry at his own weakness. Nevertheless, he wrote it again; he could not help himself. Once more he erased it, then removed the temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them.

The old man kissed her, hurried her into his room, and locked the door. Then he rushed back to the Doctor, opened the window, and partly raised the blind. Resting a hand on the Doctor’s arm, he looked with him into the courtyard.

Below stood a crowd of men and women, forty or fifty at most. There were too few of them, standing too far apart, to fill the courtyard. Those occupying the house had opened the gate and let them rush in to use the grindstone. It had clearly been placed there for them, in a spot both convenient and hidden from view.

But what terrible workers, and what terrible work!

Two men were madly cranking the grindstone’s double handle. As its turning brought their faces upward and tossed their long hair back, they looked more cruel and horrible than the fiercest savages in their most terrifying disguises. They wore false eyebrows and moustaches. Their hideous faces were covered in blood and sweat, twisted by their howls, their eyes glaring with animal excitement and lack of sleep. As these brutes kept turning, their tangled hair swung forward across their eyes and back over their necks. Women held wine to their mouths so they could drink without stopping. Between the dripping blood, the spilling wine, and the stream of sparks flying from the stone, everything around them seemed filled with gore and fire. Not a single person in the crowd appeared free of bloodstains. Men shoved one another aside to get their turn at the grinding wheel. Some were bare to the waist, their bodies and limbs smeared with blood. Others wore every kind of rag, all stained. Still others had decked themselves like devils in stolen women’s lace, silk, and ribbons, soaked through with the same red. The hatchets, knives, bayonets, and swords they brought for sharpening were all bloody too. Some of the battered swords were fastened to their owners’ wrists with strips of linen or torn pieces of clothing. The ties differed, but every one was deeply stained the same colour. As the frantic men snatched their weapons out of the shower of sparks and raced back into the streets, that same red seemed to burn in their wild eyes. Anyone whose own humanity survived would have surrendered twenty years of life to still those eyes with a well-aimed gunshot.

Joe proffered some more gravy, which I dared not accept.

“He gave you a world of trouble, ma’am,” Mrs. Hubble observed, in sympathy with my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated; “trouble?” She then launched into a dreadful inventory of every illness of which I had been guilty, every sleepless night I had perpetrated, every height from which I had fallen and every depth into which I had tumbled, every hurt I had inflicted upon myself, and every occasion upon which she had wished me buried and I had stubbornly declined to oblige her.

I fancy the Romans must have irritated each other exceedingly with their noses. Perhaps that accounts for their restless character. At any rate, throughout the account of my offences, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose provoked me so much that I longed to pull it until he roared. Yet everything I had suffered so far was as nothing beside the dreadful sensations that overcame me when the silence following my sister’s narrative was broken. During that silence everyone had regarded me, as I was painfully aware, with outrage and disgust.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently guiding the party back to the subject they had forsaken, “Pork—looked at as biled—is rich as well, ain’t it?”

“Take a little brandy, uncle,” my sister said.

Heaven help me, the moment had finally arrived! He would discover its weakness, declare its weakness, and I should be ruined! Beneath the tablecloth I clutched the table leg with both hands and waited for my doom.

My sister fetched the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured out his brandy; nobody else would have any. The miserable man dallied with his glass—lifting it, examining it against the light, setting it down—and stretched out my torment. Meanwhile Mrs. Joe and Joe busily removed the dishes to make room for the pie and pudding.

I could not turn my gaze away. Still gripping the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the wretch toy with his glass, raise it, smile, tilt back his head, and swallow the brandy. Immediately the company fell into indescribable alarm: he leaped up, wheeled about several times in a ghastly, convulsive dance of whooping coughs, and dashed through the doorway. He next appeared beyond the window, violently plunging and spitting, twisting his face into the most monstrous shapes, and apparently bereft of reason.

I kept my hold while Mrs. Joe and Joe hurried to his assistance.
